title: the bridge
hook: three nights of asking, one burst of anger, and the ocean finally speaks

segments.voice: Yesterday: the bridge, before a single stone, and your line, an army on a beach. An embrace, a march south, Rama on the shore at night asking the wind to touch her. Did you name one gap you can't see across? Today, Rama asks the ocean itself. Day six hundred thirty-five.

Rama spreads kusha grass on the sand, the sharp ritual grass, and lies down on it, facing the sea. He folds his hands. He's asking the god of the ocean, Sagara, to show him a way across. One night passes. Nothing. Two nights. Nothing. Three nights, fasting, waiting, and the water just keeps coming in and going out as if no one were there. Three nights of careful asking, and the sea gives no sign it has heard.
screen: `A BED OF KUSHA GRASS.` → `THREE NIGHTS OF ASKING.` → `NO ANSWER.`

segments.voice: On the fourth morning Rama gets up angry. Gentleness, he tells Lakshmana, is taken for weakness. He takes up his bow and starts firing into the sea. Valmiki makes it frightening: the waves heave, the sea creatures thrash, the water churns as if the end of the world had come. Lakshmana steps in and catches his brother's arm. Enough, he says. And then Rama fits a terrible weapon to the bow, ready to dry the ocean to its floor. That's when the ocean rises. Sagara comes up out of the water in person, shining, wearing garlands and jewels, with the rivers around him, and he speaks with folded hands. Here's the heart of his answer. I can't change what I am, he says. Earth, wind, sky, water, fire: each keeps its own nature, and mine is to be deep and hard to cross. I won't dry up, and I won't go still. But here is what I can do. If you build, I'll hold it up. And you already have the builder: Nala, son of Vishvakarma, the craftsman of the gods. He can do it. One problem remains. The arrow on Rama's bow can't simply be put down. So, at the ocean's suggestion, Rama sends it north, to a place of wrongdoers, and Valmiki says the land it struck became a desert. Look at the shape of this. The answer was never to make the sea stop being the sea. The answer was to work with it. The bridge isn't built against the ocean. It's built with the ocean's help.
screen: `RAMA TAKES UP HIS BOW.` · `THE OCEAN RISES.` · `I CAN'T CHANGE WHAT I AM.` · `NALA CAN BUILD IT.` · then, large: `BUILT WITH THE OCEAN, NOT AGAINST IT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breath be slow and even. Think of something or someone in your life that won't change: a deadline, a habit, a family member's way of doing things, a body that is what it is. Instead of pushing against it, ask the ocean's question. What can it hold up, if I build with it? Rest with that question. Breathe in, and let it be what it is. Breathe out, and look for the way across. The bell holds the time.
The bridge. The ocean won't stop being deep, but it promises to hold up whatever is built, and it names Nala, Vishvakarma's son, as the builder.
Your line: I'll hold it up. Today, when something won't change, ask what it could hold up if you built with it. Day six hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Rama's vigil and the ocean's answer are told in recitations of the Yuddha Kanda; at Rameswaram, the coastal town tradition links with this story, pilgrims bathe in the sea.

original.note: Sanskrit sāgara: the ocean; in the Ramayana also the ocean god, linked by tradition to Rama's ancestor King Sagara.

trapdoor: what you thought: Rama forced the sea to obey him.
what it means: the ocean answered, but kept its nature; it offered to hold up a bridge instead.
what a scholar hears: Valmiki gives the ocean a speech on svabhāva, each element keeping its own nature, earth, wind, sky, water and fire.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda 21–22 (Rama's three-night vigil; his anger; the ocean's answer; Nala named; the arrow sent north)
